idiom_name: read-check-populate helper plus store-then-invalidate write path
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: wrap the read in one helper that (1) looks the key up in the cache, (2) returns it on a hit, and (3) on a miss loads the value from the source of truth, stores it with an expiry and returns it; put the write path in one place that commits to the source of truth and only then deletes the key. The helper owns the policy - TTL, what not to cache, and how concurrent misses for the same key are coalesced - so callers never reach into the cache directly. Keep the cache outside any transaction and treat every cache error as a miss.
code_sketch:
read(key):
    v, ok = cache.get(key)
    if ok: return v
    v = source_of_truth.read(key)          # miss: load
    cache.put(key, v, ttl=DEFAULT_TTL)     # populate with an expiry
    return v

write(key, new_value):
    source_of_truth.write(key, new_value)  # store first
    cache.delete(key)                      # invalidate second
pitfalls: Reversing the write order (invalidate, then store) lets the next reader repopulate the stale value.
No TTL as a backstop plus at least one write path that forgets to invalidate.
Unbounded growth or unbounded entry sizes without an eviction policy.

Wrong move: invalidating before the database commit -> a concurrent reader reloads the pre-commit row and repopulates the entry, which then serves stale data for its whole TTL -> commit to the store first and delete second.

Wrong move: trusting the in-application delete-after-commit for correctness -> a crashed process, rolled-back transaction or dropped delete silently leaves the entry stale -> keep a short TTL as backstop and, where staleness is unacceptable, drive invalidation from the store's commit log (CDC/binlog) instead of application code.

Wrong move: eager eviction that fires before the write method runs (e.g. @CacheEvict(beforeInvocation = true)) -> the eviction races the method's own repopulation and the stale value wins -> evict after the write commits (the default) and never treat the annotation as a transactional guarantee.
